By order of the royal westindia government, the tax commission will commence to take up the capitation list on the 9th November next. The undersigned commissioners will appear at each house in the towns, where every elucidation requisite is to be given by the owner or occupier, and it is expected that every owner will appear for that purpose, either in person or representative, when the commissioners call at the houses, by which in many instances may be avoided uncertainty for the commissioners and fines for the concerned. The commissioners will afterwards meet, for the town of Christiansted, at the royal treasurer's office, where the lists are to be delivered, the needful entered in the protocols, and the capitation tax paid. The ordinance of 1 1th Nov b. 1770, 10th July 1778, 13th April 1770, 16th March 1702, and the 1st Oct. 1802, together with the governor general's placard ot ol the 1823, with the exception the instalments 10th Nov for paying the capitation tax have laid down the manner in which payment of taxes on properties in the westindies are to be paid, and the following rules are to be observeil : That iVegroes willfully not given up by their owners or by those persons in whose of the king, possession thev are, will be if and the informer, sold lor account any. The capitation tax to the royal treasury is 64sk. W. G. for each town negro and Ps. 1 32sk. for each male negro in the country, and to the land treasury Ps. 1 for each town negro and Ps 2 for each male negro in the country, to be paid thus : Capitation tax not amounting to Ps 20 immediately on taking up the list, but if Ps. 20 and above that sum, in the manner specified in the ordinance of the 11th November 1776. That negroes born or dead in the course of the year, are not taxable, but they are notwithstanding to be regularly specified in the lists þÿdelivered. All other negroes are taxable, including invalids. Exact lists of the town negroes together with increase or decrease are to be delivered to the commissioners. In like manner the

lists of the estates must be made out with a true specification of the number of acres in canes, or in any other cultivation or pasture, the number of acres not used and the number of acres entirely useless þÿ In consequence whereof, the royal governments publication of the 26ih of September 1833 is to be attended to; Fuithermore the names of the present owners, (as directed for the towns) together with the names of all the inhabitants without exception, are to be specified on the lists. For the convenience of the community, and in order to obtain as much regularity, as possible in the tax lists, schemes have been made printed by the lloyal westindia government, which schemes will be delivered gratis for the town of Christianstaed and its Jurisdiction, at the burgher councils Incassator office and in Frederiksted and its Jurisdiction at the police otfice in that town. It is a duty incumbent on every owner of a house to announce himself as such, in writing to the commission, to prevent any doubt who is to pay the house tax ; and it is further directed, that owners of houses, that have been vacant or untenanted for six months or upwards, and in consequence thereof are entitled to get a proportional reduction in their taxes, are for that purpose, to come forward with sufficient proof of their assertion, in order to enable the commissioners to observe the needful in the protocol ; in which respect the Commissioners refer to the royal Governments publication of 20th Instant.

It is to be observed, that the commission will receive no tax lists, except ihey are made out according to the above mentioned schemes, and every column properly filled up. it is however understood, that such lists are not required from owners of houses, who have only to announce themselves as such to the commission, though not occupying their housees, as in sucli cases it will be considered sufficient when they announce themselves as such, together with the names of the persons who occupy the fiouse, in writing to the commissioners. Separate lists duly signed by the owner or occupier for each house or plantation, is to be delivered to the commission notwithstanding the concerned individual might own more than one house or plantation. All houses in both towns are to be numbered, and the name of the streets to be placed on boll) sides of the cornerhouses, painted Willi white on black ground or vice versa, in a conspicuous manner, according to Governor General v. Clausens placard of the 4th January 1777.

for the following fines are to be paid and levied In case of non compliance with the above, . Ten Pieces of Eight for every list that is not rendered in due time, it be either in town or country, and proprietors, giving in lists which do not contain the explanations directed according to the beformentioned schemes will be subjected to the same line, as the lists, in such cases will be returned to them. Owners of houses in towns, who neglect announcing themselves as such in writing are liable to the same fine. 10 Ps. for every house number that is either wanted or illegible, and the same for every streets name having the same defect. For all unpaid capitation tax under Ps. 20 a levy will be made within 24 hours after the time, when the lists ought to have been delivered to the commissioners. Furthermore all persons are requested to bring the exact amount of the capitation tax to be paid to each treasury, as the time wili not allow to make change. Tax-Commission, St. Croix, loth October 1836. W. Oxholm. Erichson. Jon. C. Andrea H. M Keetsch. Wolff.

MAKETH KNOWN, that whereas the unfavorable circumstances of the planteis in the latter years have by degrees occasioned a reduction in the number and an irregularity in the mode of engaging and discharging the persons, employed on the estates as managers and overseers, which are in contradiction with earlier regulations and as inconsistent with the welfare of the community as with the maintenance of public order and security, 1 have deemed it expedient to fix certain rules with regard to the number of free persons who are hereafter to be employed on everv estate. 1 do therefore direct and order as lollows : þÿ 1. Upon every inhabited place in the country shall reside at least one free and responsible person. 2- On every sugar estate from the smallest up
No. 406. Regierings Avis. MANDAGEN den 21 de NOVEMBER 836.

to those having 125 negroes, at least 2 responsible free persons shall be employed. 3. On every sugar estate, who has beyond 125 and up to 225 negroes, at least 3 responsible free persons shall be settled. 4. On sugar estates, having beyond 225 negroes, at least 4 lesponsible and free persons shall be employed. 5. The persons thus employed upon the estates shall each in their respective situation be responsible for any disorder or disturbance, which by their neglect or fault may occur upon such estates. 6. It is a matter of course, that the above mentioned persons must be allowed to jierform any sort of work on their respective estates as far as this can be done, w ithout interfering, with or preventing them from attending to their trust. $ 7. As often as any such authorized person enters or leaves a situation upon an estate, the administrator of the same shall immediately by a written communication inform the Stadshauptman and the Police Master of it, every vacancy thus accuring shall be tilled by another person within a fortnight unless prevented by peculiar circumstances, which in such case are to be accounted for. Every free person employed on estates, shall, when changing his employment immediately report himself to his commanding officer, as ordered in the militia law. Disobedience of these orders to be punished, the first time with a fine to the poor ol 5 Rdlr v. C. second time 10 Rdlr. v. C. and to be doubled each succeeding time. 8. In case the above fixed number of free per-

sons are not employed on an estate, the owner or administrator oi' the same shall for every day lie has neglected these orders be subject to a line of 5 Kdlr v. C. to the poor for not employing a manager and 2 Rdlr v G for other persons not employed under him. 9. In case of dispute, where no written contract exists between the administrator of an estate and the diflerent employed persons on the same, three months warning from either side shall be considered legal, and in case that no contract exists concerning the amount of salary, GOO Ps. for a manager and 300 Ps. for an overseer shall be considered as legal payment, for a year's service. 10. If any proprietor or administrator of an estate should by any artifice try to withdraw himself from these orders in other respecs, than the above mentioned instances viz : þÿ by giving up persons, who by chance might sojourn on the estate, as employed by the same, he shall be liable to a fine of from 50 to 500 Rdlr. v. C. according to representation from the Police Master to the Governor General or the Governor at St. Thomas and St Johns According to the above regulations ail concerned have to conform themselves. The capitation tax to the royal treasury is 64sk. W. In like manner the lists of the estates must be made out with a true specification of the number of acres in canes, or in any other cultivation or pasture, the number of acres not used and the number of acres entirely useless þÿ In consequence whereof, the royal governments publication of the 26th of September 1833 is to be attended to; Fuilhermore the names of the present owners, (as directed for the towns) togeiher with the names of al! the inhabitants without the convenience the community, and in or- exception, are to of be specified on the lists. It is a duty incumbent on every owner ofn house to announce himself as such, in writing to the commission, to prevent any doubt vino is to pay the house tax ; and it is furl her directed, that owners of houses, that have heed vacant or untenanted for six months or up wards, and in consequence thereof are enti-

tled to get a proportional reduction in their taxes, are for that purpose, to come forward with sufficient proof of their assertion, in order to enable the commissioners to observe the needful in the protocol : in which respect the Commissioners refer to the royal Governments publication of 20th Instant. It is to be observed, that the commission will receive no tax lists, except ihev are made out according to the above mentioned schemes, and every column properly filled tip. It is however "understood, that such lists arc not required from owners of houses, who have only to announce themselves as such to the commission, though not occupying their housees. as in such cases it will be considered sufficient when they announce themselves as sucji, together with the names of the persons who occupy the house, in writing to the commis sioners. Separate lists duly signed by the owneT or occupier for each house or plantation, is to be delivered to lite commission notwithstanding

the concerned individual might own more than one house or plantation. Clausens placard of the 4th January 177 7. In case of non compliance with the above, the following fines are to be paid and levied for Ten Pieces of Eight for every list that is not rendered in due time, it be either in town or country, and proprietors, giving in lists which do not contain the explanations directed according to the beformentioned schemes will be subjected to the same fine, as the lists, in such cases will be returned to them. Owners of houses in towns, who neglect announcing themselves as such in writing are liable to the same fine. 19 Ps. for every house number that is either wanted or illegible, and the same for every streets name having the same defect. 2) AITS 31 An American Wedding. þÿ I went by invitation to a wedding at the house of a man respectable enough, though not pretending to fashion. The ceremony was performed by a Methodist parson with all proper solemnity and decorum, no man venturing among them, except the bridegroom, who sat next his bridef and the clergyman. Young men would occasionally hover about the outskirts of the cover, give a glance or even a word of recognition ; but the great body of the men adjourned into another room, where stood a table covered with plate of cakes, and bottles of wine, brandy. and whiskey ; there they made themselves comfortable : hobnobbing and joking, and letting the ladies hear at a distance how hearty they could laugh. During this time the ladies were not neglected, for the happy groomsman, as was his bounded duty, carried round the good things, and regaled them ; so it may be conjectured that they began to forment and that the contents of both rooms had only to be pouted together, like Seidlitz mixtures, in order to cause a pretty considerable commotion. At this critical period the parson summoned all to prayer, and down popped every one on their knees on the floor while an extemporary prayer was delivered, specifying particularly not only the newly married couple, but the people whose creature comfort we bad been just discussing, and other relatives accompanied as usual, with a groaning in the spirit, though in minor key and diminished quantity. After prayer, and brandy and wa-

ter excitement had arisen to such a pitch, that two or three voting men ventured to crowd into a corner among the lasses, and a mutual good understanding was the immediate consequence. I remained an observer, and soon perceived that questions and commands, and cross purposes accompanied by the most willing forfeitures, were in progress, threatening to exhaust the supply of pocket-handkerchiefs, thimbles, and penknives. At length the releasing came by the usual modes made and provided in such extremities, till kiss and come again had paid the penalties for all. þÿ Some new recruits joined in, and the games proceeded with increased spirit and rapidity like machinery works more freely after the first brush. J had just begun to think that they might as well omit the foifeits, and other forms altogether, which had fallen into sad confusion and mismanagement, and to my surprise I perceived that I had dropped exactly into their own mode of thinking, for all ceremony was sent adrift ; the gentlemen kissed the ladies, and the ladies smacked the gentlemen to their heartscontent ; and as I could hardly except any additional improvement or novelties, for the force kissing " of could no further go," I took my departure, and went homeward ponderating much on what I have seen þÿ New Monthly Magazine.

T3ST33TBI31R. CLEANLINESS. Cleanliness may be defined to he the emblem of purity of mind, and may be recommended under the three following heads! as it is a mark of politeness, as it produces affection, and as it bears analogy to chastity of sentiment. First, it is a mark of politeness, for it is universally agreed upon, that no one unadorned with this virtue, can go into company without giving a manifold offence: the different nations of the world are as much distinguished by their cleanliness, as by their arts and sciences ; the more they are advanced in civilization, the more the)' consult this part of politeness. Secondly, cleanliness may be said to be the foster-mother of affection. þÿ Beauty commonly produces love, but cleanliness preserves it. Age, itself, is not unamiable while it is preserved clean and unsullied ; like a piece of metal constantly kept smooth and bright, we look on it with more pleasure than on a new vessel cankered with rust. I might further observe, that as cleanliness renders us agreeable to others, it makes us easy to ourselves, that is an excellent preservative of health ; and that several vices, both of mind and body, are inconsistent with the habit of it. in the third place, it bears a great analogy with chastity of sentiment, and naturally inspires refined feelings and passions ; we find from experience, that through the prevalence of custom, the most vicious actions lose their horror by being made familiar to us. On the contrary, those who live in the neighbourhood

of good examples, fly from the first appearance of what is shocking: and thus pure and unsullied thoughts are naturally suggested to the mind, by those objects that perpetually encompass us when they are beautiful and elegant in their kind. In the Fast, where the warmtiiof the climate makes cleanliness more immediately necessary than in colder countries, it is a part religion of > the Jewish law, (as well as the Mohammedan> which in some things copies after it,) is filled with bathings, purifications, and other rites of the like nature; and we read several injunctions of this kind in the Book of Deuteronomy# þÿ Addison.

SHERIDAN. From WraxaWs Memoirs. As Lord Surrey secured his own seat for Carlisle, so Sheridan surmounted all opposition at Stafford, and re-appeared in the new House of Commons by Fox's side. He pos" sessed a ductility and versatility of talents which no public man in our time has equalled; and these intellectual endowments were sustained by a suavity of temper, that seemed to set at defiance all attempts to ruffle or discompose it. Playing with his irritable of angry antagonist, Sheridan exposed him by sallies of wit, or attacked him with classic elegance of satire ; performing this arduous task in the face of a crowded assembly, without losing for an instant either his presence of mind, his facility of expression or his good humor. He wounded deepest, indeed, when he smiled ; and convulsed his hearers with laughter, while the object of his ridicule or animadversion was twisting under the lash. þÿ Pitt and Dundas who presented the tairest marks for his attack, found by experience that though they might repel, they could not confound, and still less could they silence or vanquish him In every attempt that they made by introducing personalities or illiberal reflections on his private life and literary and dramatic occupations to disconcert him, he turned their weapons on themselves. Nor did he, while thus chastising his adversary, alter a mulcle of his own countenance; which, as well as his gestures, seemed to participate and display the unalterable serenity of his intellectual formation, Rarely did he elevate

his voice, and never, except in subservience to the dictates of his judgment, with the view to produce a corresponding eflect on his audience. Yet he was always heard, generally listened to with eagerness, and could obtain a hearing at almost any hour. Burke, who wanted Sheridan's nice tact and his amenity of manner, was continually coughed down ; and on these occasions he lost his temper. þÿ Even Fox often tired the house by the repetitions which he introduced into his speeches. Sheridan neter abused their patience. þÿ Whenever he rose, they anticipated a rich repast of wit without acrimony, seasoned with allusions and citations the most delicate, ye1 obvious in their application. At this period of his life, when he was not more than thirty three years ol age, his countenance and features had in them something peculiarly pleasing ; indicative at one of intellect, humor, and gaiety. All these characteristics played about his lips when speaking, and operated with inconceivable attraction ; for they anticipated, as it were, to the eye, the effect produced by his oratory on the ear ; thus opening for him a sure way to the heart, or the understanding. Even the tones of his voice, which were singularly mellifluous, aided the general eflect of his eloquence ; nor was it accompanied by Burke's unpleasant Irish accent Pitt's enunciation was unquestionably more imposing, dignified, and sonorous. Fox displayed more argument as well as vehemence ; Burke possessed more fancy and en-

thusiasm ; but Sheridan won his way by a sort of fascination At thirty-three, it might be said of his aspect, as Milton does of the fallen " angel's form, His face had not yet lost All her original brightness." Excesses of wine had not yet degraded its lineaments, eclipsed its fine expression, covered him with disgusting eruptions, and obtained

T33T3ST3D131R SilK 9TJTJi,J5T for him the dramatic appellation of Bardolph. At sixty he reminded trie of one of the com" panions of Ulysses, who, having tasted o Circe's 'charmed cup,' instanlly " And downward fell into a grov'ling swine lost his upright shape, ' Those persons, and those only, who have frequently seen Sheridan at the two different periods to which 1 allude, can form an adequate conception of the metamorphosis produced in his appearance by repeated and habitual intoxication. It would bave been fortunate for his fame, if Horace's invocation to the God of Verse, to grant him, " nec turpem seneetam Degere, nec cithara carentem," had been accomplished in Sheridan. At the dissolution of parliament in 1812, having failed to secure his re-election at Stafford, he ceased to sit in the house of commons; a circumstance most inconvenient to him as his person was no longer protected from arrest, while his debt aecumulated. I have been assured from good authority, that the Prince of Wales (or, more properly to speak, the Regent) transmitted him the sum of three thousand pounds, in order to enable him to procure his election for some other borough ; but Sheridan pressed by domestic exigencies, diverted the money to his own private necessities. From that period, during the four or five concluding years of his life, he, who had so long attracted the attention of an admiring public, insensibly became, if 1 may so express mvsslf, half-eclipsed, and in a manner forgotten while still alive. Incapable of extricating

himself by any efforts of genius or application (such was his habitual indolence) from his pecuniary embarrassments, he could no longer defy a host of importunate tradesmen who clamorously demanded payment. Like Jaffier, he might say that his doors were " ll.rred and dammed up by gaping creditors B A friend of mine, a young man, having been arrested iu August, 1815, for a debt, and carried to a spunging house, in Fetter lane, there found himself detained in a large apartment with Sheridan and Sir Watkin Lewes. The latter had been lord mayor of London, as well as one of the members for that city in successive parliaments. They remained shut up together for three days, at the end of which time Sheridan procured his liberation. He was morose, taciturn, and gloomy before dinner, for they all ate and slept in the same room ; but when he had drunk nearly two bottles of wine, as he regularly did, after dinner, he became apparently cheerful and communicative. Sir Watkin, at near fourscore, exhibited equal good humour and equanimity of mind. Declining gradually under the attack of chronic diseases aggravated by excess, Sheridan's last scene holds up an allecting and painful subject of contemplation. A privy counsellor, the ornament of his age and nation, caressed by princes and dreaded by ministers; whose orations, and whose dramatic works, rank him among the most distinguished men of his own or of any period ; expired, though not in a state of destitution, like Spenser, like

Otway, or like Chatterton, yet under humiliating circumstances of pecuniary embarrassment. His house in Savillerow was besieged by balifl's ; one of whom pressing to obtain entrance, and availing himself of the moment when the front door was opened by a servant in order to admit the visit of Dr. Baillic, who attended Sheridan during his last illness, that eminent physician, assisted by the footmen, repulsed him and shut the door iu his lacc.

ATT3 Dr Baill ie, I have been assured, refused to accept any fee for his advice ; and Earl Grey, who had so long acted in political union with Sheridan as a member of opposition, supplied him with every article for his comlort, prepared from his own kitchen. Nor, as I have heard, did the Regent forsake him in his last moments. If my information is correct, his royal highness sent him two hundred pounds ; but Sheridan declined its acceptance, and returned the money. Thus breathed his last, a man of whom it might be justly said, as of Lord Verulam, that he was " The greatest, wisest, meanest of mankiud !"

We regret most sincerely that we cannot find owe message from Gen. Jackson, not even his last, which we can say will meet the approbation of the country. That his partizans will throw up their caps and shout " hurrah," is a matter of course, for they act mechanically ; but party apnrobation is one thing, and the honest, spontaneous offering of all parties is quite another The President any day can have the use of his mechanism. We did hope his last message would have other than this mechanical approbation. What the President has to say of our Foreign Relations is very well, though so far as the N. E. Boundary is concerned, it would seem right after an eight years negociation, 'fiat he should know more of the " precise grounds" on which the dispute is to be brought to an adjustment. What is said of Texas and Mexico is much more delicately managed than we feared it would be. Indeed the President seems rational enough till he approaches the finances of the country, but then that "monster" the U. S Bank, as has been the rase this seven years, seems to throw his reason off its equipoise, and to affect all else he lias to say. The Bdl distributing the Surplus Revenue he does not recommend a repeal of, as some seem to have imagined that he would, foi on the 1st January, the present law expires, and 'n order to be a new distribution there must be a new law. Hence, as we have all along been aware, that he would, the President in order to prevent the passage of a new law, strikes at the principle of this, and proposes a

disturbance of the Bill of Comprise between the North and South. The President, however, throughout his remarks, acts upon this erroneous idea, that some body approves of creating a Surplus Revenue in order to distribute it. The question is, " what shall be done with a surplus when it exists ? and it is but a delusion of the people to present any otlwr before them. The Government wish to lock it up in the coffers of the Banks. The people wish to have it at their own disposal. The Tariff is not the matter in dispute. The President says, there will be upwards of 41 millions of surplus which, with the exception of 5 millions, will be transferred to the several Stales, &c. What says the author of the doctrine of the spoils, Silas Wright, to this? Will he tell the Senate again, and gel his friend Benton to back his statement, that there will be no surplus, as lie stated when the distribution bill was under debate ? What says the Globe to this ? Let us compare these authorities with the matter of fact. Where is Mr. Woodbury's Boston letter? W e now approach a part of the message, which we know not how to treat with that respect due to a document emanating from the President of the United States. Carrier Pigeons, are thus trained: At eight or ten weeks of age they begin to run, or to make (lights of four to five hours from the nest. They are then strong enough on the wing to commence their education. The pigeon to be trained is first taken no greater distance than a mile fromc home, and tossed into the air ; when, after flying round and round, and rising soine height into the air, it wings its way back. This lesson is repeated live or six times in as many days. þÿ T he bird is then carried to the distance of two miles, and tossed. þÿ This lesson is repeated twice The bird is next carried three miles, and tossed ; and this lesson is likewise repealed two or three times. The bird is then carried six miles, and then twelve, then twenty four, then forty-eight, then ninety six, and so on, in geometrical ratio Each of those lessons is given once only. The longest flight that a carrier pigeon lias been known to make is eight hundred miles. In so long a flight the bird is supposed to pitch at night and roost, renewing its flight the following day. When a trained carrier pigeon is tossedi after making one or more circles, it rises in a rapid spiral to an enormous height before it takes its departure, and at that height it is supposed to make its journey. þÿ Boston Transcript.

false Swerrriwr. þÿ A remarkable case occurred once in an English Court A suit was brought by an heir-at-law, to recover possession of an estate of which the defendant had been several years in possession, as legatee tinder a will, purporting to have been executed some fifteen years before the death of the testator. This was alleged by the claimant to be a forgery. In support of it, a very aged man, who had been steward to the testator, and whose name appeared upon the will as a witness to its execution, was produced at the trial and examined. His appearance was vc- Durable, and his testimony was so clear and positive, that it wrought conviction in the minds of judge and jury, and even of the clainiants counsel. In the course of a long and rigoious cross examination, no wavering, no

TasTisrasx aaoaaauwoa A-rita, shadow even of contradiction, could be elicited At length he mentioned a circumstance which, the defendant's counsel said, would put all doubt at rest. The testator, when he put his seal to the will, had placed upon the parchment a silver six-penny piece, and covered it with wax ; and the counsel broke the wax and produced the coin. The judge was about to call upon the jury for an immediate verdict in favor of the defendant, when the plaintiffs counsel, who bad been closely scrutinizing the coin, started suddenly up> said that the will was indeed a forgery þÿ called the judges' attention to the date stamped upon it. w hich w as of a year long subsequent to the date of the will. The old witness fell back, and was taken out of the court room, and died in the course of the next day. Miss Edgeworth has introduced this incident almost verbatim in one of her novels. þÿ N. Y. Com. Speaker and Gentlemen ; Deeply impressed with a sense of the responsibility devolving on me, I cannot injustice to myself repress the emotions ol my heart or restrain the feelings which mv sense of obligation to my fellow-citizens, has inspired þÿ their suffrage was gratuitously bestowed Preferred to others, possibly superior in merit to myself, called to the most important station among mankind, by the voice of a free people, it is utterly impossible not to feel impressed with the deepest sensations of delicacy in my present situation before mankind. It is not

here alone, but our present attitude betoie all nations, has rendered my position and that of the country, one of peculiar interest. A spot of earth almost unknown to the geography of the age þÿ almost destitute of resources þÿ comparatively few in numbers, we modestly remonstrated against oppression ; and when invaded by a numerous host, we dared to proclaim our Independence, and to strike for freedom on the breast of the oppressors. As yet our course is onward We are only in the outset of the campaign of Liberty. Futurity has locked up the destiny which awaits our people. Who, with apathy, can contemplate a situation so imposing in the physical and moral world? None! þÿ no, not one. The relations among ourselves are peculiarly delicate and important: for no matter what zeal or fidelity T may possess in the discharge of my official duties, if I do not obtain co-operation and an honest support from the co-ordinate departments of the government, wreck and ruin must be the inevitable consequences of any administration. If then in the discharge of mv duty, my competency should fail in the attainment of the great objects in view, it would become your sacred duty to correct my errors and sustain me by your superior wisdom. I his much I anticipate þÿ 'his much I demand. I am perfectly aware of the difficulties that surround me and the convulsive throes through which my country must pass. I have never been emulous of the honors of a civic wreath, when merited it crowns a happy destiny. A

country situated like ours, is environed with difficulties, its administration fraught with perplexities. Had it been my destiny I would infinitely have preferred the privations, the toils of a soldier to the duties of my present situation. Nothing but zeal stimulated by the

In the attainment ol this object, we must regard our relative situation to other countries. A subject of no small importance to our wellare, is the situation of an extensive frontier, bordered by Indians, and subject to their depredations. Treaties of peace and amity and the maintainance of good faith with the Indians, present themselves to my mind as the most lational ground on which to obtain their liiendsliip Abstain on our part from aggression, establish commerce with the different tribes, supply their useful and necessary wants, maintain even handed justice with them and natural reason will teach them the utility of our friendship. Admonished by the past, we cannot injustice disregard our national enemies. Vigilance w ill apprise us of their approach, a discipline d and valiant army will insure their discomfiture. situation, as the rich diamond looked in the bosom of the adamant. We cannot hope that the bosom of our beautiful prairies will soon be visited with the balmly breezes of peace. The course which our enemies have pursued has been opposed to every principle ol civilizea warfare þÿ bad faith, inhumanity and devastation, marked their path ol invasion. We were a little band, contending for liberty j þÿ they were thousands, well appointed, munitioned and provisioned, seeking to rivet chains upon us, or to extirpate us from the earth. þÿ Their cruelties have incurred the universal denunciations of Christendom. The family of the Rothschilds have assembled at Paris. Their house, it is said requires, reorganization, and Paris is henceforth to be the centre of their operations. The line of operation already extends to Constantinople, St. Petersburg, and Madrid ; and London is only a subordinate point from which their dealings radiate We are rather struck with such a description of this great banking family, as giving to their proceedings a military character. At least they are described in military language ; and we can conceive the Rothschilds runuing along their lines ot operation, and liberating Prince Metternich at Vienna, or shutting up the Emperor Nicholas with his armies at St. Petersburg. Louis Philip they wiii be close to, and lie will not be allowed to stir without their permission. We trace their power in his negotiations; two bankers connected with Switzerland have been sent to Berne. They seem to be more powerful than even was Bonaparte; for, by means of the sea, our brave sailors completely protected us from him, but they cannot keep out the Rothschilds. þÿ Courier.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE ANTIGUA HERALD, Mr. Editor, Having occasion to go to Windward yesterday 1 was exceedingly surprised to see the immense quantity ol Ants which infest the whole line of road from North Sound to Nonsuch. These ants, I was informed by a respectable manager, have done much injury to the estates in the neighbourhood of Betty's Hope, in consequence of their feeding on the bud ol the plant as soon as it begins to germinate Knowing the interest you take in every thing connected with the welfare of the agricultural part of the communiy, 1 have sent you the following recipe, for the destruction of these insects. It is copied from " A Treatise on the cultivation of the Sugar Cane, By W. Fitzmaurice," and 1 beg that you will transcribe it into your valuable journal. " Take a small quantity of arsenic, and mix it with a few ounces of flour or oatmeal, moistened with a little molasses. Place a lump of this compound, (about the size of an egg) on a flat board, covered with a wooden bowl or box and put several of them in dillerent parts of the plantation. The ants will soon take possession of them, and the poison will have general eflect, for those ants that die are always eaten by the others, so that the estate will soon be effectually clared of them." Hoping this plan if adopted will succeed in preserving the ensuing crop from innovations of a similar nature. 1 remain, Mr. Editor, your Most Obdt Servt. Nov. 17, 1836. A. 1'.

TROOPS IN THE WEST INDIES. The augmentation of the 1st West India Regiment, from 639 to 1009 rank and file, has enabled the Government to withdraw two regiments from the forces in the Leeward Colonies, thereby considerably reducing the expenditure for our troops in that part of the world, and diminishing the casualties among our European soldiers. It is now proposed to garrison with the 1st West India Regiment those stations that have proved most destructive to white troops, such as Berbice, Tobago, St. Lucia, and Dominica. In the latter place the left wing of the 79th Regiment lost in eighteen months 74 men, or one third of their complement, not that the seasons of 1834 or disadvantages of the island are such, that mor- tality to a great extent among any white 83 were particularly unhealthy, but the local 1 troops quartered there. The mainguard have to march from their barracks on Morne Bruce to the forte, down a steep and harrassing hill, and so encircled by lofty mountains that the heavy rains come on so rapidly and unexpectedlv, as to baffle every precaution ; þÿ the consequences are obvious þÿ in marching down the men drenched in rain, and must proceed to relieve guard in their wet clothes. Arrangements ought to be made for them to take a change of linen in their knapsacks, and which plan was adopted by that excellent officer Gapt. G b, of the 76th Regiment ; but will they change the garments now partly dried upon them ? we are afraid that four men out of seven would avoid the trouble, and re-

main for twenty four hours imbibing the seeds of fever and dysentery. But even if, by good luck, they escape a tropic shower when marching down, the chances are, on returning from guard mounting, they are thoroughly soaked with rain, and, on being dismissed at their barracks, would they change their inner garments ? certainly not, when a turn in the sun on the parade ground and a glass of rum at the canteen sets all right again. The garrison at St. Lucia is below par when compared with Dominica ; and no European soldier, when it can be avoided, ought to be allowed to mount the break-heart hill of Mcrne Fortune. True, þÿ exercise is necessary lor the preservation of his health in the tropics, but to oblige him to toil for an hour and a half, laden with his arms and accoutrements, up a precipitous, nay almost inaccessible mountain, now sinking under tiie influence of a broiling sun, and shortly afterwards drenched with rain, is certainly one way of acclimatising him, but we fear that, like the horse, when reduced to live upon a straw a day, he will die under the experiment. Both of these desirable posts ought to he garrisoned by black soldiers, who would perform the duty equally well as Europeans, and with comparatively little loss to themselves. Essequebo, Demerara, and Prince Rupert's Dominica, are each held by acompany of the 1st West India Regiment ; of the last Golgotha it is sufficient to say, that in the year 1809 and 1810 the garrison frequently buried 85 men weekly, and

a fatigue parly was told off every day to dig pits in the swamps for patients expected to die in the hospital during the night ; as it is. even with the black troops inured to the place, and from long service almost "children of the mist," one-fourth are generally on the sick list. What a grave this would be to þÿEuropeans. Naval and Military Gazelle.

The mutability of fortune is thus beautifully described, 1 may say drawn, by the pen of Kennedy, in his late address before the American Institution : ' Our country is a country of busy men. Whatever gives facility and expansion to labor, benefits every class of the community. Unlike the European States, we have no piles of hoarded wealth to be transmitted in mass to our posterity Opulence, among lis is like, a gilded pyramid that stands upon a pedestal of ice, and its foundations are perpetually melting in the sun : the stream that flows from them may fertilize the land and spread bloom and beauty over barren places ; but the pyramid itself falls in its appointed time, to be built up again bv other hands and to adorn other cities. Our laws, which forbid the accummulation of hereditary treasure, have reiterated to the American citizen, "said sentence of an ancient date" þÿ toir, og that, "like an Emmett, he must ever toil" þÿ and they have promised to labor fulness of honors. In providing, therefore, for the industry posterity of we hut hew out for ourselves and our posterity a better and more auspicious destiny.'

O'Suilivan, Esq.; who came passenger in the ship Alfred, from Cadiz, we obtained the following verbal intelligence, the ship having brought no papers; " The army of Gomez, the Carlist General, which had been ravaging the province of Andalusia for three months, and baffling all the troops of the Queen, by which it had been constantly surrounded, was at length destroyed in a battle near Medina Vidonia, almost wiihin sight of Cadiz. Gomez had made an unsuccessful attempt to retire to the Tagus, but was prevented by the presence ofRodil, the Minister of War, with a large force interposing. Rodil was recalled to Madrid to answer for misconduct in not bringing Gomez to action. His army was left in command of General Narvaes, who eammanded in the battle of the 25th and 26th, near Cadiz, Espinoza was superseded as Captain General of And. lusia, by Ordonez, his second in command. ' Gomez had twice entered and sacked Cordova, took Almaden by storm, threatened Serville for nearly a fortnight He marched down to Algesiras, where he had a slight action, in which an English frigate from the Bay, took part in favour of the Queen's troops ' It was reported at Cadiz, when the Alfred left, that Gomez had been taken prisoner. His army was entirely dispersed, and the prisoners were being brought into Cadiz." þÿ Times.

bills of exchange. An Act of Parliament has just passed which settles a disputed point in regard to bills of exchange, and which ought, therefore, to be known to men of business generally. The point alluded to is that respecting acceptors or referees for honour, in which no uniform practise existed, some houses presenting the bills so marked on the day which they became due, and others on the day after. It is now declared, howeve, that it shall not he necessary to present such hills of exchange until the day following that on which they became due, and if the address of the acceptors or referees for honour, shall be in any other place than that in which the bills should be made | ayable, they need not be forwarded until the day succeeding that in which they became due. If the following day should be either Sunday, Good Friday, Christmas day, they need not be presented or forwarded until die day succeeding such day of non-business.

\e.w Invention. þÿ A late London paper describes the following invention: A new machine for taking casts has been lately invented by a gentleman in Paris, and is called the Physiognotype. It is of a verv simple nature, and takes an exact imprint of the countenance, without any disagreeable sensation, by an application of less than two seconds. This instrument is a metallic oval piate, pierced with a large quantity of small Holes, very close together, and through each of which a metallic wire passes with extreme facility. 1 hese needles have the appearance ol a brush. 'I he whole is surrounded with a double case of tin, which contains waim water, in order to keep the instrument of a pro cr temperature with the blood, Ifanv figure be applied against this brush of needles, it yields to the slightest pressure, and leaves an exact mould. The needles arc then fixed by a very simple process, and from this metallic mould the cast is taken. It is, in fact, a new application of the principle of a process familiar to sculptors, by w hich a fac-simileof a

model is obtained in marble, the needles being driven into the stone. There is nothing disagreeable in the application of the instrument; but the sensation cannot well be described, although, if the Physiognotypc were not heated, it would feel like immersing the face in snow. The impression left is an undoubted likeness, and the mask which it produces is a fac-simiie of the mould. Nothing is wanting þÿ even a vein on the temple is faithfully represented.

Some twenty years ago, when in retired parts of the country the communication between one place and another was much slower arid less frequent than it is now, there was a great deal of horse stealing carried on in the English counties on the borders of Wales. þÿ Those counties were and are very full of pretty little towns and villages, in one or another of which there were fairs for the sale of live stock almost every day of the year, and it was easy to steal a horse from one parish, and carry it away and sell it at some one of these fairs, almost before the rightful owner knew that he had lost it. Well, it so happened that about this time lived a lazy, careless> rollicking sort of fellow, by name, Morgan Jones, who contrived to make a living somehow or other, but how it was nobody wel| knew, though most people suspected that it was not the most honest livelihood a person might gain In fact, every body was sure that .Morgan was deeply implicated in horse, stealing, and many a time had he been brought before the Just'ce on suspicion, but do what thev could, nobody could find sufficient evidence to convict hiin. People wondered and talked about it for a long time, until at last tliey came to the only natural conclusion þÿ namely, that Morgan Jones must have dealings with the evil one Now it once chanced that Morgan and some of his chosen cronies were making themselves jollv over sundry pots of ale and pipes of tobacco, at a round white deal tablet

in the clean parlour of a very neat little ale house, as all village ale houses arc in that part of the country. And they began to get very happy and comfortable together, and were telling one another their adventures, till at last one spoke plainly out, and told Morgan Jones that it was commonly reported he had to do with the devil. ' Why, yes," answered Morgan, "there's some tiuth in that same, sure enough ; I used to meet with him now and then, but we fell ont, and 1 have not seen him these two months." " Ay!" exclaimed each of the party, "how's that Morgan ?" "Why then, beqniet, and I'll tell you itall." And there upon Morgan emptied his pot, and had it filled again, and took a puff of his pipe, and began his story. "Well then," says he, "you must know that 1 had not seen his honour for a long time, and it was about two months ago from this that I went one evening along the brook shooting wild fowl, and as I was going whistling

k'jr. »' am mm' m ' / ' along, whom should I spy coming up but the devil himself ? But you must know lie was dressed mighty fine, like any grand gentleman, though I knew the old one well by the bit of liis tail which hung out at the bottom of his trousers. Well, he came up, and says he, ' Morgan, how arc you V and, says I, touching my hat, ' pretty well your honour, I thank you.' And then, says he, ' Morgan, what are you looking a'ter, and whats that long thing ye'ere carry with you ?' And, says I, I'm only walking out by the brook this tine even" ing, and carrying my backy-pipe with me to smoke.' Well, you all know the old fellow is mighty fond of the backy ; so, says he, ' Morgan let's have a smoke, and I'll thank ' ye.' And, says 1, ' you're mighty welcome So I gave him the gun, and lie put the muzzle in his mouth to smoke, and thinks I, ' 1 have you, now, old boy," 'cause you see 1 wanted to quarrel with him : so I pulled the trigger, and off went the O 'run bans' O in his mouth. ' Puff !' says he, then pulled it out of his mouth, and lie stopped a minute to think about it, and says lie, D þÿ ' d strong backy Morgan !' Then he gave me the gun, and looked huffed, and walked off, and sure enough I've never seen him since. And that's the way got 1 shut of the old gentleman, my boys !" Such is the ludicrous story of Morgan Jones, who had to do with a proper Welsh devil, without doubt.

christianity Forbids no necessary occupations, no reasonable indulgences, no innocent relaxations. It allows us to use the world, provided we do not abuse it. It does not spread before us a delicious banquet, and then come with a " touch not, taste not, handle not." All it requires is, that our liberty degenerate not into licentiousness, our amusements into dissipation, our industry into incessant toil, our carefulness into extreme anxiety and endless solicitude. So far from forbidding us to engage in business, if expressly commands us, not to be slothful in it, and to labour with our hands for the things that be needful ; it enjoins every one to abide in the calling wherein he was called, and perform all the duties of it. It even stigmatizes those that provide not for their own, with telling them that they are worse than infidels. When it requires us " to be temperate in all things it plainly tells us, that we may use all things temperately ; when it directs us, to make our moderation known unto all men, this evidently implies that within the bounds of moderation we may enjoy all the reasonable conveniences and comforts of the present life." Bishop Porteus. þÿ

New Bee Hive. þÿ An inhabitant of Connecticut, Mr. Judd, has invented a contrivance by means of which bees are made to build their cells and deposit their honey in the chain, ber of a dwelling house in neat little drawers from which it may be taken fresh by the owner, without killing the insect. The Norwalk Gazette describes it as follows : þÿ þÿ The hive has the appearance of, and is in part, a mahogany bureau or sideboard, with drawers above and a closet below, with glass doors. This case or bureau is designed to be placed in a chamber of the house, or any other suitable building, and connected with the open air or outside of the house by a tube passing through the wall. The bees work and deposit their honey in drawers When these or any of them are full, or it is desired to obtain honey, one or more of them may be taken out, the bees allowed to escape into the other part of the hive, and the honey taken þÿaway. The glass doors allow the working of the bees to be observed ; and it is added that the spaciousness, cleanliness, and the even temperature of the habitations provided for them in this manner, render them the more industrious.

SATURDAY being the anniversary of the birth of our most gracions and well beloved Sovereign FREDER1K YIth. who on that day entered his 70th year ; it was announced at Sunrise by the discharge of Koval Salutes from the Batteries of Fort Christiansvcern & from His þÿMajesty B s rig AUert, Capt. Kier Iff \ which Vessel was most elegantly decorated with Flags, from Sunrise to Sunset. At 1 1 þÿo Clock, the troops of the Garrison and the different Militia Corps of this part of the Island, under Lieut. Col. Peter de Xu/ly, (K. ot d.) Sladshauptman, were assembled on the Parade Ground, and soon after 1 1 is Excellency Governor General von Schoi.ten, attended by a numerous Suite, arrived on the ground, and taking a station in front of the line, exclaimed þÿ Ltenge leve Kong Fkedekik den þÿSjette which was responded by three hearty cheers, and by a Koval Salute of 27 guns from the field pieces of Christiansted's Artillery, and a feu de joic by platoons along the whole line þÿ His Excellency then taking the command, the troops were reviewed in inarching order, and went through many evolutions in military style, much to the gratification of the numerous spectators present. At 1 þÿo Clock a Levee was held at the Government House, and His þÿMajesty health s was drank accompanied by Koval Salutes of 27 guns from Fort Christiansvcern and His þÿMajesty B s rig AUert. In the evening, a very numerous Levee took place at the Government House, and a sumptuous Supper was provided, and the evening was spent in great hilarity, and much

to the satisfaction of the numerous company and strangers, who were present, þÿ a profusion of Champaignc was served to all, during the evening ; the health of our beloved Sovereign was again drank in bumpers, and the following Song composed for the occasion was sung with great animation by the whole company. His þÿMajesty s Brig Alle.rt, again fired a Royal Salute in the evening, and made a brilliant display of Koekets, Blue Lights and þÿfire-works, much to the gratification of numerous spectators. The company separated at a late hour, highly gratified, and filled with ardent wishes, that the life of our good King may be prolonged many years in health and happiness.

In our last Gazette we announced the arrival of the 1st December packet from Eng. land ; the second followed close upon her heels, the mail having arrived the day after the first. By the London Times of the 15th December, we learn of the defeat and retreat of the formidable expedition under Marshal Clausel, destined to capture Constantino, a city laying 40 Leagues S E. of Algiers and governed by a Bey formerly tributary to the Dey of Algiers. Marshal Clausel had marched from Bona with 20,000 men about the middle of November; þÿ after many difficulties and very rainy and bad weather, he succeeded in reach' ing Constantine, (a þÿwall city d and well lortified) ; with his advanced guard of 7,000 men þÿ he expected to carry it by a þÿ coup de main'' but found them well prepared, the þÿ red flag hoisted, and his appearance saluted with Cannon Shot from the walls. After an ineffectual cannonade from the few heavy pieces of Artillery he had been able to bring forward, Marshal Clausel found himself under the necessity of retreating, harrassed by the Arabs ; and his dispatch is dated at three days march from Constantine, in which he acknowledges the loss of 3,000 men out of 7,000 by the exposure of bivouacking in cold rainy weather, þÿ in fact bis dispatch resembles some of the famous French bulletins from Kussia> during the campaign of 1812, þÿ the Duke de Nemours, son of the King of the French accompanied the expedition, þÿ reinforcements from Toulon and Marseilles had been sent

him after news of the disaster hud reached France, þÿ the Arabs were well provided with Artillery, the result of this expedition toge- þÿ ther with the bad state of affairs in Spain, it is thought, would occasion a change of ministry in France, and that Marshal Soult and Al. Thiers would be again reinstated. In Spain the war assumes more activity. þÿ Bilboa still held out, it was closely invested bv the Carlist General & Commander in Chief Villareal with 20,000 men under liis command ; þÿ a part of which force was employed under Eguia in attacking the town and a part to prevent the approach of the þÿQueen Gene- s ral Espartero, who had advanced for the re. lief of Bilboa with 10,000 men, and w ho had been repulsed in the attempt. Eguia had pushed his advances nearly into Bilboa, and that place being cut off from supplies from the Sea, it was feared it must soon surrender ; þÿ a most gallant defence had been made by its garrison. Espartero was within a league of Bilboa at the lust dates. Gomez again succeeded iri evading Narvaez after the battle of 20th November; þÿ Ins superiority in Cavalry enabled him to escape with 4 or 5 000 men, and he was marching upon Murcia ; þÿ his plan being to put under contribution every town attached to the Li bo" ral cause of which he could get possession, three armies were in pursuit of him.

Airis In England the conservative interest appeared to be gaining ground ; þÿ the breach between the YVliigs and Kadicals daily becoming greater, the new registration of voters being much in favour of the Conservatives (according to the Times), it was thought a new election of the house of Commons would give that party a majority. Sir Kobert Peel had been invited to public Dinners at Edinburg and Glasgow. Money affairs were rather improved in England, in consequence of the assistance afforded by the Bank of England A report of a Committee of the Cortes to treat with the South American States, had been accepted by that body, and it was thought treaties would soon be made acknowledging their independence. The will of Charles X. had not yet been opened, the presence of all the Koval family being required on the occasion, the Courts of Vienna, Munich and the Hague had adopted mourning, for the deceased Monarch; the Duke de Bordeaux, it was said, was about proceeding to St Petersburg on a visit, and reports of a matrimonial engagement between him and a daughter of the Emperor of Kussia were current. The London Times credits reports of Ihe partial insanity of the Emperor Nicolas. His Koyal Highness Prince Christian of Denmark, was expected to visit Paris in Janu. ary, and London in the following months. The Archduchess Theresa of Austria was to set out for Italy, accompanied by her illustrious father the Archduke Charles, and she was to be mairied to the King of Naples, early in January.

Lord Melbourne had lost by death, bis only son, much regretted by his noble relatives. The London Times from the 1st to l(th Dec. are full of details of the damages done by the storm of 29th November; every town in the South and West of England having suffered more or less by its ravages ; þÿ it was also as severely felt in the towns in the North of France, in Belgium, Holland, Hamburg, Kiel, and all along the Danish Coast þÿ by those who have experienced West India Hurricanes, the violence of the winds was said to be similar to them in the storm of 29th November, but much more damage was done on the land, than among the shipping at sea. The ex-Queen Horlense intended proceeding to the United States, to rejoin her son Prince Louis Bonaparte þÿ she was about sell, ing her Estate in Switzerland ; the Government of that country having intimated their intention not to permit her residence there any longer, in consequence of suspicions of her being a party to the late attempt of her son to excite a revolt at Strusburg The trial of those engaged in that plot was to take place early in January. The Vcndomc trials had already commenced. It had been intimated to Prince Louis Bonaparte that the Government of France intended pursuing the same course towards him as that adopted by his uncle Napoleon in the case of the Duke þÿD Enghein. This greatly alatmed him, but on his expressing great sorrow and regret at bis being led into the attempt, he was permitted to embark for the United States.

The Reindeer þÿI ackotarrived here on the afternoon of Wednesday about 1 þÿo clock, from windward, and sailed on Thursday alternoon at same hour for England, with mails from the Islands, hut without any from Jamaica þÿ The Lord Melville remains in the harbour, waiting the arrival of the Steamer from Jamaica with mails, after which she will proceed for England. An Official Notice appears in the Barbados papers, stating that, in consequenc of a communication from the Naval Commander-inchief, the Ports of New Granada are placed under strict blockade, by His Britannic Majesty's ships of war in the West Indies. The brig Serpent sailed from Barbados on the 23rd January, for Leeward, and the Melville 74, Admiral Hai.ket, on the 25th for Carthagena. The steamer now expected, will likely bring us some information with regard to the dispute about the affairs of the British Consul at Panama, so long back as January 1836.

On Saturday Baron Verduille de Feuillas, editor of La France, was brought to trial before the Court of Assizes, upon an indictment for attacking the constitutional order of succession to the throne ; for opposing the rights which Louis Philippe holds by the will of the nation, and for adhering to a form of government different from the established regime, in an article published by that journal on the death of Charles X., in which the Due Angouleme is repeatedly called King of France. The breach between France and Austria appears to grow wider every day. The News from Brest and Toulon is full of animation ; every ship of war in either port is fitting out for sea, and the naval preparations, whatsoever may be their destination, are on a truly grand scale. The doubts with regard to the fidelity of the army are not removed ; a late order takes away the mali.e, or portmanteau, from the sub officers of even the most favoured regiments. From Boll's Messenger. DEATH OF CHARLES X. We deeply regret to announce tl at letters reached Paris on Monday afternoon with in. telligence of Charles X. having departed this life on the Oth instant, at Goritz, in Illyria, whither the royal family had just transferred their residence from Prague. On the 4th St. þÿCharle s-dav, his þÿMajesty fete s was celebrated by the friends and servants who had faithfully adhered to his fallen fortunes; and on the next day he is stated to have been attacked with an inflammation in the bowels, which has put an end to the life of as good, amiable, and well-intentioned a man as ever ascended a throne, or political animosity ever drove from one. Though fate selected him as a victim of her several trials þÿ though thrice an exile from the palace of his ancestry, and the sport of circumstances, which are more powerful than human will þÿ he preserved the respect and esteem of those who were about him to the last, and exhibited a moral dignity in his misfortunes which well became the high lineage from which he has descended. A few attached subjects rendered him the homage of their loyalty and their love, though the world had abandoned him, and his own kindred had conspired to blot his name out of the list of European sovereigns. There still remained some honorable men whose loyalty was above price, whose affection was increased bv bis misfortunes, and he was perhaps more proud, and more happy, in their support, than when millions bowed down before his throne, and

sycophants sought honours and distinctions at his hand. The Count þÿd Artois, as Charles X. was called during the life of his two elder brothers, quitted France previous to the last terrors of the revolution, and took a distinguished part in the military operations which were undertaken with Prussian aid on the northern frontier. He then removed to the shores of Great Britain þÿ the hospitable refuge of all men like him, whose virtues are illustrated by their misfortunes. He occupied the Palace of Holyrood for some time, and then resided in South Audley-street, Grosvenor-square, for several years, happy in the society of one for whom he had made great sacrifices, and whose attachment was of that romantic nature which scarcely belongs to this age of hard reality. Previous to the revolution, as one of the hondsomest men of his day, he dipped deeply into all the pleasures and excitement of that gallant time, and lived witli so much profusion that he contracted debts, for which afterwards he was persecuted in this country. Among the many curious adventures in which lie was engaged, his duel with the Duke do Bourbon þÿ whoso mysterious death a few years since must still be fresh in our readers recollection þÿ was not the least remarkable. þÿ The Count d'Artois was present at one of those magnificent masked balls which were then given at the Opera house, with the beautiful Madame de Cadillac under his protection- Their attention was drawn to the splendid costume of another mask, whom they suspect-

ed to be the Duchess of Bourbon, then living separated from the Duke. Madame de Cadillac went beyond the bounds of etiquette in trying to gratify her curiosity ; and the Count d'Artois, so far forgot himself as to aid it by attempting to remove the mask from the face

of this distinguished personage. The consequence of this freedom was that the Duke of Bourbon felt himself obliged to take the matter up. A challenge was given and received þÿ and the two princes of the blood met in the Bois de Boulogne with their repective seconds. The Duke de Bourbon was one of the best swordsmen in France, and he received with perfect composure the violent assault of the Count þÿd Artois, contenting himself with parrying his thrusts, and not taking advantage ol his own power, or of the unskilfulness ot his opponent, but the seconds being military men soon perceived it, ami those in the suite of the Count þÿd Artoisadvanced between tlie combatants, and called on their principal to remark that the Duke de Bourbon had not taken advantage of the opportunities which circumstances had afforded. The Count, on hearing this, threw away bis sword, and, rushing into the arms of the Duke, offered him every atonement that, he could require, and asked again to be restored to his friendship. The Duke warmly embraced the Count, and then returned to Paris in the same carriage. Such were the French gentlemen of that day ! The Count þÿd Artois married, before the revolution, a daughter of the House of Savoy, but, having bad the misfortune to loss her, he formed an attachment with Madame de Pol lastron, the sister of the Prince de Pelignac, whose misfortunes are at present occupying the attention of the public. His affection for this lady was so sincere that when she died,

during his residence in South Audley street, he became a prey to the heaviest grief, and a remarkable change came over his mind and character. Previous to that period he had been distinguished for acts of gallantry, and habits of life which will not bear strict criticism : but from the hour of Madame de Polþÿlastron s death he became thoughtful and reserved, and sought in the religion of bis forefathers a consolation for the blow which bis affections had received. The Count d'Artois was always generous, spirited, and amiable ; but now a fresh motive excited bis good nature, and the acts of bis charity became unbounded. His benevolence was as silent as it was sincere, and many a þÿwidow and s orþÿphan s heart have been made glad without knowing the source of the bounty to which they were indebted. While thus fulfilling the duty which his devotion prescribed, and which his own feelings dictated, lie did not neglect the claims which the gentlemen of France who abandoned their country with him had on his family. He was the friend and associate of all the distinguished emigrants þÿ the warmth of his manner gaining every heart, the more so as it was contrasted with the colder and more calculating spirit of his elder brother. To be a Frenchman and an exile þÿ was a passport to bis friendship. He was one of the first of the royal family who returned to France on the restoration. þÿ He appeared Vatessoul, in Franche Comte, in 1H14, and soon afterwards passed on to Paris,

where be acted as Lieutenant General ol the kingdom, to which he had been instantly appointed by Louis XVIII. It was chiefly through bis exertions that the claims of emigrants were taken into consideration ; and the indemnity which was voted for their use, and part only of which they received, in consequence of the legislative plunder of M. Lafitte, in 1831, was mainly attributed to his exertions. A love justice of v\ as the foundation of his character and compensation þÿ to those who sacrificed everything for his family was in his iniud a sacred duty- lie ascended

the throne on the death of his brother, Louis X VIII. The revolution of 1830 is fresh in our þÿreaders recollection, &, we need notgo over the circumstances of that unhappy period. '1 he. events which have since occurred have rendered justice to the motives of Charles X., and of the ministers who have, up to this time, been made the victims of a policy vindictive as it is unjust. The spirit of republicanism which has so often attempted to overthrow the monarchy that succeeded bis was nabugbeai of the imagination. Unfortunately for his family, the measures he adopted were unequal to the end. He was the victim of a conspiracy which had been long organised. England again received the illustrious exile, and Holyrood once more sheltered him from the political storms of the revolution. Let those who wish to write the private history of Charles X. go to Holyrood for materials. The respect and affection of the people in that neighborhood for him and the illustrious companions of his exile are the best evidences of his virtues. Since Charles X. thought fit to change his residence from Great Britain to the Austrian States, he lived in the vicinity of Prague, occasionally visiting the celebrated baths of Tceplitz, or occupying in the summer a chateau near the former city. He there devoted all his thoughts to the education of tfie illustrious prince who is the heir to the virtues, but we hope not to the misfortunes of his family. þÿ Watching over the young scion of a dynasty of eight centuries, the exiled monarch has spent

his time in patience and resignation, forgetful of the past, forgiving the many wrongs which he sustained from an ungrateful people, and filling the mind of bis tender charge with the purest love for France, and with an awful sense of the high duties which the same fate which deprived him of a throne may cail upon him one day to exercise. W ithin a few months he determined to remove from Prague, and established the ruins of his fortune and household at Goritz, in Illyria ; but scarcely had be made the change than the hand of death came to summon him to that place where the monarch and the subject are equal, anti where all the cares of his former state, and latter wrongs, are hushed in eternal sleep. He died in the midst of the members of his afflicted family, whose constancy and truth long compensated him for the injustice of the world.

BIOGRAPHY OF MARTIN VAN IJIJREN. (From the Pennsylvanian .) Martin Fan Buren was born at Kinderhook, in the county of Columbia, and state of New York, on the 5th December 1782. In early boyhood he displayed endowments so superior, that his father resolved to educate him for the law, a science for which be evinced both fitness and predilection. Although his time, during this period, was chiefly engaged bv bis studies, and by the other duties of a law student, yet as lie grew up be could not fail to be interested in the exciting political events which marked the close of the last century. His father, who had been actively devoted to the American cause during the" Revolution, had espoused the principles of the democratic party on the formation of the National Governmenr, anil was among the earliest supporters of Mr Jefferson when he became its leader. His son early adopted the same sentiments, and his course secured for him such confidence with the neighbouring democracy, that while yet young in years, he took a part in the contests of the day, as active and efficient as that of veteran politicians. He completed his legal studies in 1802, and commenced the practice of the law in Columbia county, first at Kinderhook, and afterwards at Hudson. He soon raised himself to the highest rank in the profession, and was admitted rival and equal ol the ablest lawyers in the state. v In 1812 he was elected, for the term of four years, to the senate of New York, in which body he took his seat in the following Novem-

ber. He at once promoted and supported every measure calculated to aid or strengthen the general govern nent in carrying on the war. In the spring of 1813, he wrote an address to the electors, issued by the Republican members of the legislature, in which lie enforced with energy and eloquence, as well as with effect, the duty of sustaining the administration with all the resources and influence of the state. In the year 1814, the political friends of Air Van Buren regained their ascendancy in the House of Assembly, and his efforts were consequently attended with greater success. Of these, the most prominent, as it was certainly the most energetic ever adopted in this country, was a law, framed with reference to property as well as persons, for raising immediately, through the agency of classes, 12,000 men, to he placed at the disposal of the general government. His ability and reputation, both as a lawyer and politician, now deservedly indicated him for the office of Attorney General ol the State, and to that he was accordingly appointed in February, 1815 He was also chosen about the same time one of the regents of the University, and soon after removed his residence to Albany. In the revolutions of party politics, one so distinguished could not avoid some reverses ; and those with whom he acted hav. ing, in the year 1819, lost the controul of the appointing power, he was removed from the office of Attorney General. It was not long, however, before he was summoned by Isis fel-

low-citizens to a station of higher interest. þÿ He had for some time warmly advocated a convention for amending the State Constitution, which he considered defective in many particulars. A law for the convocation of ed. one was passed by the legislature, and it assembled at the capitol in the year 1821. Mr Van Buren, though a resident of Albany, was, unexpectedly to himself, returned as a member by the electors of Otsego county, and took his seat as tiieir representative. His speeches in the convention are evidences at once of his ability, and of the soundness, moderation, and justice which characterised his opinions on the various principles of government brought into elaborate discussion. From the convention Mr. Van Buren was called to represent his native state in the senate of the United Slates. He continued in the senate for more than seven years, being reelected on the expiration of his" first term, "and in that enlarged field displayed the same abilities. and soon acquired the same elevated rank, which he liad acquired in tho more
