limted sphere afforded by the councils of his own state. In the discussions of all t he great questions of public policy, his opinions were promptly and ably expressed The consistency and decision which had early secured the confidence of his friends, still distinguished him. Throughout the eight years, during which Mr Van Buren occupied his seat in the senate, witli this eminent distinction, lie continued to receive increased marks of the confidence and affection oi his fellow-citizens at home. 11 is services were appreciated, and his principles were approved. When the period arrived for electing the governor of the commonwealth, lie was brought forward with enthusiasm as the democratic candidate for that office, and chosen with the most flattering marks of public approbation. He of course resigned his seat in the senate, and on the 1st ot January, 1829, entered upon his new office. His administration was short, but it was marked by a successful effort to introduce salutary provisions for the independence and security of elections : and still more by financial reforms among the most striking and important in the history of the United States. When General Jackson became President of the United States, he immediately nominated Mr. Van Buren to the first place in his administration, as Secretary of State. This office lie accepted and resigned that of Governor. A large portion of each branch of the legislature ot New York, consisted at the time oi his political opponents ; yet such had been his up-

rightness and ability, that resolutions expressing the high respect for his virtues and talents, and tendering him. in warm and affectionate terms, the good wishes of the representatives of tlie people, were in both unanimously passed. M r. Van Buren repaired to Washington and on the 12th of March, commenced the discharge of his new duties, as Secretary of State. The records ol his administration will show, that at no previous period of the government was there as much official labour periormed in the same time, or successful results to so many negotiations, as during those two years ; arid even though the credit of this be awarded, as it justly may be in an eminent degree, to the high character, perseverance, and courage ot the chief magistrate under whose views ot policy Mr Van Buren acted, he is yet entitled to great merit for the talent, fidelity, and zeal lie displayed, in assisting to produce these brilliant consequences. The long contested colonial question between the United States and Great Britain, which had been suspended by the preceding administration as hopeless, was resumed, elaborately discussed, and finally adjusted, on terms previously sought by the United States, New negotiations were opened with France, relative to our claims lor commercial spoliations, which had existed for more than twenty years, and also to tier demand of commercial preferences under the eighth article of the treaty of Lousiana Both of these were thoro gly investigated under the instructions ot Mr. Van

Buren. and the whole matter settled by treaty, in a manner highly satisfactory, very shortly after he left the Department of State. Den mark had presented her ultimatum in respect to similar claims of our citizens, which had not been accepted ; negotiation was resumed under new instructions, and an adjustment effected uy which an indemnity, nearly fourfold larger than that previously offered, was secur- Spain had positively refused redress for her depredations upon our commerce, and so pertinaciously adhered to her system of discrimination. that all negotiation on the subject had ceased ; the question, however, was again opened under new arid very full instructions from Mr Van Buren ; the matter was ably and vigorously prosecuted by his successor; a satisfactory indemnity was secured ; and notwithstanding the proverbial re pugnance of the Spanish government to make any change in its commercial policy, it was induced to consent to an abolition of "discriminating duties, and to the adoption of the regulations offered by the United Slates in ali nations. Indemnity was obtained from Portugal for depredations upon our commerce, and she consented to repeal the prohibitory duties which she had for a long time imposed upon our rice, in favour of that of Brazil, Efforts,

commenced by Mr. Jefferson, and continued through the succeeding administration to place our trade with the Levant on a favourable and permanent footing, and secure a passage for our shipping to the Black Sea, were revived, and a treaty concluded with Turkey, which lias given stability and prosperity to our commerce, in that interesting portion of the world. A negotiation opened by the preceding administration with Austria was brought to a satisfactory conclusion hv a commercial treaty. For many years it had been an object to form a commercial treaty with Russia, and repeated attempts to do so had been made ; these were renewed ; a minister was despatched to that country with instructions in which the whole subject was fully examined ; and the view s of the United States were communicated without reserve. Through adverse circumstances, this effort failed of success at the time: but when Mr. Livingston succeeded Mr. Van Buren, lie renewed it with complete success. With Mexico our affairs were found to be in the worst condition. The ratification of a treaty already concluded had been suspended in the Mexican congress ; jealousies and suspicions of an aggravated nature had been excited against us : and such was the position of affairs, that the respect guaranteed to the diplomatic character was actually violated in ihe person of our minister. A new minister was despatched to Mexico; the injustice and impolicy of her course were strongly and unreservedly point-

ed out ; and difficulties, which threatened an immediate rupture, were removed in sueli a manner as to uphold our dignity and rights, and place the relations of the nations on the best footing of which they were susceptible. With the republic oi Columbia similar difficulties had arisen The iiead of that government had become impressed with the belief that we were unfriendly to his country and to himself, and this feeling had been communicated to his official associates. Its effects were seen in the unfriendly temper manifested towards our minister, in a refusal to listen to the just claims of our citizens, and in the imposition of prohibitory duties on flour, our chief export to that part of South America. þÿ A minister was sent with full instructions prepared by Mr. Van Buren on all these subjects, and his mission was attended with complete success. Good feeling was restored, the American claims were in a great degree adjusted, the exorbitant duties on flour were reduced to the standard proposed by our government, and tiie most liberal relations in all respects established. Having thus administered this important and laborious department for about two years, Mr. Van Buren determined to retire from that honourable trust In June. 1831, he resigned the office of Secretary of State, with the reluctant consent of the President, by whom lie was soon after appointed minister to Great Britain. He wTas received by that Government witli that favour and distinction to which

the high offices lie had previous held gave him, periiaps more than usual claims, and he commenced under the best auspices the interesting negotiation which he believed would he, if successful, ns useful to his country as honourable to himself. While thus employed abroad, his nomination was submitted by the President at home to the senate for their constitutional advice and consent ; unfortunately for the honour of our country, that body, hitherto respectable, was at that time selected as t he field fur the display of principles and conduct utterly at variance witli the expectations oi tlie American people. Three aspiring politicians, who had already received striking proofs of tlie disapprobation of their countrymen, though previously advocating the most opposite opinions, united a coalition, the design of which was to force themselves into power and to defeat, if possible, the prospects and success of a man, in all respects their superior, and as much entitled to the honours tie had won, as they were unworthy of those which they sought A majority of tlie senate was found sufficiently servile to sustain tlie views of these individuals, and to unite with them in a selfish crusade against tlie cause, and the advocates of popular measures. By this majority thus formed, actuated by motives the most unbecoming, and on pre

©AST texts the most weak and trivial, the appointment of Mr. Van Burcn was negatived, alter protracted dehates and delays, on the 25th of January, 1832. The measure was etleetod by the casting vote of John C. Calhoun, then vice-president of the United States; a politician whose career was marked by inconsistencies so gross, and an utter dereliction of patriotism, and principle as a public man, that this act, whether arising from his judgment or his envy, seemed only to be wanting, in order to prove the sterling virtue, talents, and character of him whom he thus vainly endeavoured to thwart in his onward and honourable course. In consequence of this event Mr. Van Huron returned at once to the United Stales. He returned to a people equally able and disposed to protect those who are faithful, and to punish those who are treacherous ; to a people who viewed witli indignation the unprincipled conduct of the senatorial coalition, and who determined at once to manifest that indignation, in a manner not to be misunderstood. As the period for electing a vice-president of the United States was at hand, they resolved to place Mr. Van Buren in the station which had just been so grossly abused bv the person who held it. and called him to preside over that very body, and those very men who had fruitlessly exerted their accidental power, for their own selfish ends, not merely against him, but the people who loved him, and the principles he had always maintained. In November, 1832, he was elected by an

overwhelming vote, and in March following, he entered on his public duties as President of the Senate. His address on that occasion elicited the applause of all parties, and its moderation was rendered the more conspicuous and honourable, from the circumstances of his rejection to which we have alluded. His term of service will expire on the 4th of March, 1837 ; but it having been ascertained that President Jackson, following the example of his predecessors, would then retire from public life, a numerous body of delegates, representing the democratic party of the Union, assembled at Baltimore in the month of June, 1835, and unanimously presented him to the people of the United States, as a candidate for the chief executive office.

GRENADA. (From the Free Press.) We have received a circular containing an account ol the advantages likely to be derived from the compost manure for sugar and cofice, prepared by James and Thomas Brown, of London. A hogshead of this ' very cheap manure" is described as giving "agicat return, and with little labour,' contains about "one ton, and is sufficient for one acre of cane land, by sewing a small quantity in each hole at the time of the first weeding; and upon a worn out soil." No. þÿ2 of the circular which we have given entire, is worthy the attention of the Planters in this Island No. 1 þÿ Extract of .a letter from Montserrat addressed to Messrs. Ncavc, Broad Street, London, dated July 30th, 1830. " The Compost Manure docs exceedingly well at Dagnarn. What was sent out last year is the strongest and the best kind ever sent, and I am sure that, with favourable weather, the Plant canes that have received it, will give three large Hogsheads of Sugar per acre. I also observe, that the (dials from the Canes that have had the benefit of it at all times are great, and give a large return of Rum. It would be a great advantage to send out eighteen or twenty hogsheads to I.. G. Estate, where there are only thirty two head of Cattle to make manure." From the same, Dated 2nd April, 1831. "1 have the satisfaction to say, the Compost Manure is now producing three Hogsheads of Sugar per acre, notwithstanding the great disadvantage ol a long continued drought." Mr. Mc'Leod, from St. Vincent's, says bis

method with the Compost Manure is, to apply it to the first rattoon, which then gives a return equal to the Plant Cane with Pea manure; and in situations where the saving ot labour is essential, and upon poor land, the advantages are very great. The Coffee Tree should have two pounds of the Manure spread and raked in over the roots; it will work down of itself. Besides Sugar and Collee there may be other articles of valuable product, with w hich we arc acquainted, but to which this fine Manure might he very serviceable. We have been informed, that the Managers upon some of the Estates, where the land is very poor, do use as much as live hogsheads of the Compost Manure upon four acres of 'Jane land, and that quantity is found sufficient to make an ample return.

From the great improvement in this manufactured Manure, and reduction in the price, is now found to be both cheap and serviceable. £ 4 10s. per Hogshead, free alongside, package included. By JAMES & THOMAS BROWN, Limehouse Out London, N. B A very cheap Manure, making a great return and with little labour.

No. 2. þÿ The Compost Manure, for home use, is made to protect the Turnip Plant from the Fly, and which would in all probability protect the Sugar Cane from the insect which is so destructive to it. It is very strong but being packed close in a hogshead, would not be objectionable in the Ship. Neither is it likely that there would be any objection to its being landed when in a hot climate, for there is nothing fetid or unwholsome in it, only that it has a very powerful effluvia when exposed upon the land. Hares will not come into the Fa-Id where it is used, and Rats may have an equal aversion. It is 20s. per Hogshead dearer, namely, £ 5. 10s., free alongside, package included.

The composition is now ofibred for lite first time to public notice as being applicable to all Out door buildings. Piles for Bridges, Dock and Canal Gates, and every description of Wood and Iron Workboth as a Pi/mciit and a Preventive of Decay. To Ship owners in particular, it is especially recommended, tot only as it adheres readily to w l plank.- but because, in const quetice ol its dr\ in <_> in a few hours, it may be applied between tides. This varnish is cheaper than any other article in n-e, and must on becoming known supersede Tar and perhaps even copper itself, possessing in itsell the elasticity of the one with toe solidity of the other. Mrs. Child related to me the following touching anecdote : þÿ " A clever young Physician, of the name ol VVallis, went from Alexandria to a town in the slate ol .Mississippi, and look up

his aboard in a hoarding house. Here he fell in love with a very beautiful young female, who had the management of the establishment. Siie was slightly coloured, but not having sufficient prejudice to prevent liirn appreciating her worth, he made her an oiler of his hand The oiler was accepted, they were married rather secretly, and he brought her as his wife, into the district of Columbia. They had not been very long man and wife, when one day an individual, dressed in the garb of a gentleman, called upon Dr. Wallis. Alter some little conversation the man, in a very grutl voice said, " Sir, did you not bring a woman from the south with you?" ' No Sir,' replied Dr VVallis, ' l'am not aware that I did,' ' Why,' retorted the other, 'did you not bring your wife from the south?' 'Yes,' replied Dr. Wallis, ' 1 believe my lady is from t lie South.' ' Your lady, as you call her, is my slave, and unless you give me 900 dollars for her at once, 1 will advertise her as a runaway slave. She is honestly worth 1,000 dollars, but as you have married her, 1 will let you have her for 900. Struck with astonishment, Dr. Wall is said, ' your slave, I don't believe it.' ' Believe it or not,' replied the other, ' you will find it correct ; I shall leave the hi, I, and if you do not send the money to me before such a time to sucli an hotel (naming the time and place) I will advertise her in the papers as a runaway slave.' As soon as the man was gone, Dr. Wallis went up stairs to ins amiable lovely and accomplished (tor by this

time lie had given the finisli to a previously imperfect education) wife, and said, ' My love, when 1 married you, were you a slave ?' She burst into tears, and faltering said, ' I was.' ' And why did you not tell me this before we were married ?' ' I did not dare to tell you,' she replied; 1 feared you would never think of forming an alliance with a slave.' 'Well,' ' 1 have found you out, but 1 will give the 900 dollars, for 1 love you far too well ever to part with you.' During this time she was very deeply agitated, and requested Dr. Wallis to describe to tier the individual who had claimed her as his slave. He gave her as accurate a description of the man as he could, and then asked her it it corresponded with tier former master. ' Yes,' said" she, ' and more than my master ! that man is my own lather?'

a shout story am) a tri e one. A lovely morning in October, 17 þÿ , was rendered a gloomy one to the inhabitants of Martinique. Repeated injuries inflicted by the ruling powers, coupled with a burning desire among many ambitous and, perhaps patriotic men, to crush foreign influence upon

their beautiful isle, and to govern themselves as a free and independent people, had long rendered a residence there precarious. On the morning in question, the banner ot revolt was seen floating in proud defiance upon the walls of the castle of Fort Rot a', and in the far distance the smoke of villagers showed the track of the merciless demon ot insurrection. Every vessel in the harbor of Fort Royal was crowd' d with refugees, who, having hastily collected their most valuable effects, bad fled before the tide of destruction which was rolling fearfully over that ill-starred island. Among tlmin was a merchant of high repute, who with his wife and daughter, a beautiful girl of about fifteen, took passage for France, whither on the following day the vessel sailed þÿ Fair winds gave them a quick passage to the Cape de Verds, and after a tarry of a day or two they weighed anchor for Havre. At dawn on the second morning after their departure they espied a dark looking brig bearing down upon them, and as the sun rose above tiie horizon, it portrayed to tiiein the truth that an Algcrine corsair was their early visitor. So much were the high seas infested at tiiat time with pirates, tiiat every vessel went prepared for an encounter. Immediate preparation was made for a contest, should the corsair overtake them, and all sails were spread to the breeze. The pirate came up þÿ the contest was fearful þÿ the father and mother were murdered þÿ > and the beautiful orphan was made the prize

of a band of ruffians. In a few days they neared the Barbary coast, and she was sold to the Bey of Tunis for ten thousand sequins. The prediction of a fortune teller, years before, that she would one day wear the coronet of a queen, impressed on her mind with a conviction of its truth, which spread a halo of light round her amid the darkness of the worst of slavery. Her beauty made her a fav orite, and about two years afterward, Sultan Mustapiia carried her in triumph to Constantinople. Her beauty, her virtues, her am, !e powers to please, made her the exalted favorite of the imperial seraglio, and she became the honored Sultana. Then indeed were the predictions of her destiny verified, and she wore the crown as queen of the Ottoman empire. Mahmoud II., the present Sultan of Turkev is her son, and to her influence upon his early character may be attributed his taste for European customs, and the frequent innovations which his will has made among the customs of Ins people. The last act of importance, and which seems like a great stride toward tiie elevation of Turkish women to the same station which women hold throughout Christendom, is the opening of the doors of the seraglio, and permitting the women to go in and out at their pleasure, and enjoy themselves by upon the lovely plains which stretch along the banks of the lovely Bospliorus The number who were confined in his seraglio was about six hundred. The late of that young girl was similar to that of Josephine, wife of Napoleon. She too.

was the subject of a similar prediction, and even when confined by prison bars, and upon the eve of conveyance to the guillotine, that prediction stood up before her with all the brightness and sacredness of Truth ; and when the downfall of Robesperrie caused her prison to be thrown open, " There." exclaimed she to Madame Fonteany, a fellow prisoner, " i told you I should yet be Queen of þÿFrance." And she was indeed Queen, not only of France, but of the heart that beat in the bosom of that proud Corsican who swayed its destinies þÿ I'oughkecpsiu Telegraph,

London January 16. þÿ We this day present our readers with the details of the splendid Banquet given to Sir Robert Peele at Glasgow þÿ a temporary building or theatre was erected 127 feet square, containing tables to accommodate 3,500 persons; the inside of the building was lined with 8.000 yards of white cotton cloth and elegantly decorated for the occasion, and lighted up with superb chandeliers< the height of the h til was 35 feet, the tables being placed on an inclined plane, gave each one a fine prospect of the whole company- This building cost £2,000 stlg. þÿ Three tables erected on a platform about 4 feet higher than the floor, were reserved for the most distin" guished guests, and were superbly decorated with gold and silver plate þÿ 3.500 persons sat down to dinner the first toast drank was þÿ " The King" followed by the National anthem of " God save the King" sung by the whole company ; and when the lines " Confound their politics," " Frustrate their navish tricks " were repeated, immense cheering followed. When the toast " Our distinguished guest Sir Robert Feete" was announced, the cheering lasted 15 minutes, and was so tremendous as to shake the whole nuilding þÿ after which Sir Robert arose, strongly affected with these marks of w lcomc--in an eloquent and elaborate speech he gave an expose of Conservative principles, portrayed the dangers of adopting successing Reform and declared his firm determination to adhere to that Cons' buttonwhich guaranteed the King, the Lords, and

the Commons in the rights and priviledges which they now possessed. þÿ Sir Robert was frequently interrupted with great cheering, and sat down at the conclusion of his speech, amid the most animated applause. No accident attended the festival, and the numerous party separated at a late hour, much gratified with the arrangements which had been made to honor their distinguished guest.

The news of Espartero's victory and relief of Bilboa caused great rejoicings at Madrid þÿ by a decree of the Queen Espartero had been creaied a Grandee of Spain with a new title- The city of Bilboa in addition to " loyal and victa, or " unconquerable þÿ noble" was to add to these designations, in- " the Queen promises to make good to its loyal inhabitants all losses sustained by their heroic defense. þÿ Votes of thanks were passed in the Cortez to Espartero and his army, to Col. Wilde and to the naval officers and forces of England, and to the inhabitants of Bilboa, þÿ the attack of the 29th December was made in a snow storm, in the afternoon ; this, covered ihe approach of tue assailants þÿ w ho carried all the heights called Las Baiideras ; þÿ Espartero heading the columns of attack þÿ the battle lasted late in the night and next morning þÿ the Carhsts having made live unsuccessful attempts to regain the heights the loss of the þÿ Queen's army is stated at 1,000 men, the Carhsts in their retreat buried the mortars employed in the siege of Btlboa, but they have been recovered by the Queen's army, 8,000 of Espartero's army were to relieve General Evan's Legion at St. Sebastians, leaving the latter at liberty to resume the offensive.

PROGRESS OF STEAM NAVIGA- TION, &c. The last half century has been eminently fertile in political changes, but these will in all probability be surpassed in moral and social importance by the changes which the next half century will witness, arising from causes of a very different nature, and wro.ught out by peaceful and blameless means. Railways and steam navigation are instruments of social advancement, the full effects of which no man can forsee, though all can perceive that their extension is fraught with a vast addition to the resources of mankind, and a vast increase of the means of enjoyment. Circumnavigated by steam boats, and intersected in all directions by railroads, a communication between the most distant parts of Great Britain will shortly be the work of only a few hours, and thus will at once be realized all the advantages to be derived from a dispersed and a concentrated population. The effect of steam navigation, with regard to the distant possessions of this country þÿ the outlying provinces of the British þÿempire for as such they ought to he considered þÿ will be no less striking and important Many have speculated upon the possible fate of our vast dominions in the East, and of the changes which they would experience in our hands. But there is one change which a few vcars ago no one would have ventured to predict. No one would have entertained an idea, even in a dream, that we should bring these rich dependencies nearer home þÿ yet this will steam navigation for all practical purposes,

enable us to effect. While the natural and geographical positions of ihe countries remain the same, their social and commercial relations will undergo a change equivalent to that which would be effected by a local approximation. No wonder, then, that both in India and in England such a warm interest should have been excited in favour of the establishment of a regular communication bv steam. We know that interest to be increasing, and we are persuaded that before the meeting of Parliament the expression of it will become so loud and universal as to render it altogether irresistible. þÿ Atlas.

THE YOUTH OF GEN. JACKSON. >#<«- General Jackson was born on the 15th of March, 1767, in South Carolina, in the district called Warsaw Settlement. His father was an Irish emigrant, who had come to Charleston two years before, and who died shortly after the birth of Andrew Jackson, leaving a widow. During the boyhood of young An. drew, his mother often related to him the part which his grandfather had taken in the defence of Carrickfergns, and the oppressions exercised by the Nobility of Ireland upon the multitude. These traditions made a deep impression upon the mind of yonnat Andrew. He had been destined for the Church, but at fourteen years of age he accompanied his brother into the canto during the levolutionary war, and was made risoner with him. While in captivity an English officer, I appening to order him, in an imperious tone, to clean his boots, Andrew refused, saying that he was a prisoner of war. and not a servant. In reply the officer struck him on the arm with his sword. It was his first wound, and also t ho end of his first campaign, for he soon niterwards recovered his liberty. At eighteen yeais of age he definitely renounced the Church, took to the law in 1786, and pleaded in North Carolina ; but about year a and a half afterwards he was seized with a desire to emigrate, and establish bintself in Nashville, in Tennessee, where he soon became Attorney General ol his district. In 1196 he was nominated a member of the Convention lor arranging the Constitution of the State of Tennessee, and in 1797 was elected member of

the Congress. He remained so, only two years, resigning in 1799, and was chosen one of the Jtt- gcs of the Supreme Court. But he found that civil employment did not suit him, and soon resulted this new office also. He was then thirty-three years of age At this epoch the State of Tennessee formed the extreme frontier of the Union ; it was the refuge ot all adventurers from the East; its population w as composed of men of activity and enterprise, hut rude and uncultivated in their manners, and who lived in a w ild independence upon their half-cleared territories. As they were continually exposed to attacks from the Indians, every one for his personal safety carried a dagger and a brace of pistols, which were often employed against other adversaries than the Hedskins or the beast of the forest- Nothing was at that period more common than the quarrels decided, breast to breast, on the instant, with the dagger or the pistol. þÿ These ferocious manners have by degrees disappeared Tennessee, in and it is now only in the extreme confines of the Mississippi or Alabama that it is usual to see guests shooting at each other across the table, and killing their neighbours on the right or left. Tfierc the morning question still is, " Who was stabbed last night?" as in other quarters information would be asked about the price of merchandize. It is still common in the valley of the

Mississippi to wear dirks, arid often in the steam-hoat the astonished traveller espies a pair of pistols in his companion's girdle It was precisely during the youth of Andrew Jackson that Tennessee and Kentucky were the theatres of these exploits, and the General, being of an impetous courage and a fiery temperament, ready to take umbrage on the slightest occasion, and eager to espouse the quarrels of his friends when he had none of his Own, it is not surprising that he signalised himself in this stormy society. Without be. lieving all that is related of him, it seems certain that whenever there was an interval of repose in the hostilities against the Indians, disputes with his own companions were indispensable to him. His rencontre with Colonel Benton is cited in the United States as one of the characteristic episodes of the early manners of the West. The following is the account publicly given by Colonel Benton of the conflict of himself and his brother with Gen- Jackson and his friends. As the statement of an adversary, it must not be considered as convicting General Jackson, but rather as a picture of the manners of that time. Indeed, I the Colonel lias since acknowledged that Gen. j One house had at this time last year, wheat Jackson was not entirely in the wrong, by show ing himself one of the most devoted partisans of his Administration : þÿ " Franklin , Tennessee, Sept. 10, 1813. " A misunderstanding which lias existed some months between General Jackson and

myself had on Saturday, the 4th instant, at Nashville, a result unexampled in a civilised country. In making my friends and fellowcitizens acquainted with this afiair, 1 shall confine myself to the principal facts, which I am ready to authenticate in a Court of Jusiice: þÿ First, when 1 arrived here with my brother, we went to a different hotel from that at which I was 40,190,000 pounds, and to Europe only General Jackson lodged, in consequence of I 35,824,000 pounds. his threats of personal violence. Second, the j General presented himself with some of his j friends at our hotel ; he commenced by taking aim at me with a pistol, although I was unarmed, and advanced towards me without giving nie time to seize one. 'lhird, seeing this, my brother fired at the General, w hen the latter was about eight or ten feet from me. Fourth, four pistols shots were then fired þÿ one by Gen. Jackson at me, two by me upon him, and the four by Colonel Coffee at me. In this discharge General Jackson was wounded, but 1 was not touched. Fifth, we then took to daggers þÿ Colonel Coflec and Mr. Donaldson threw themselves upon me, and wounded me in five places. Captain Hammond and Mr. Hays attacked my brother, who, weakened by a previous wound, could not maintain himself against two He was thrown on the ground and, while Captain Hammond prevented him from rising, Mr. Hays attempted to stab him. My brother was severely wounded in both arms while parrying the blows, and was finally rescued from this critical situation by a citizen

of Nashville. .Sixth, my pistols and those of my brother were charged with two balls each. The pistols discharged at me were fired so close that the explosion of one burnt the sleeve of my coat, and the other was aimed at my head at only arm's length. The attack took place in the house where the Judge of the district, Mr Searcy, was staying, so little res. pcct had our adversaries for the law or its officers. The civil authority has not yet taken cognizance of this disgraceful outrage. (Signed) " Thomas HaRt " Lieub-Colunel, 49th Infantry."

ROYAL DECREE. The principal negociations, which from the beginning I so benevolently received, having been happily terminated, as 1 had efficaciously endeavored to complete the conciliation between Spain and Mexico, and being desirous, as well as the authorities of that countrv, to anticipate the benefits of peace and reciprocal commerce of two people that never ought to have ceased to consider each other as brothers, I have decreed as Q, ieen Regent, in the name of my august daughter the Queen Isabella II., what follows : þÿ 1. There is no more hostility to be undertaken or carried into effect on the part of my Government or any of its subjects against Mexico, its citizens, or inhabitants. 2. The Mexicans who are already or may come to establish themselves in Spain are to be treated and considered as the subjects of a friendly Power, and in a manner corresponding with the noble character of the Spanish nation. 3 The Mexican merchant ships will be admitted like those of friendly nations in all Spanish ports open to foreign commerce, subject to the laws and existing regulations. Palace Dec. 29, 1836. (Signed by HER M \JESTY.) To Don Jose Maria 'Jalatrava, President of the Council of Ministers.

From the, Barbados Mercury, Feb. 14 1837. By the brig Clara, Captain Longmire. which vessel arrived this morning from St. John's, New Brunswick, we regret to learn that a great portion of that town has been destroyed by a fire which commenced on the night of the 14th January last, and burnt throughout the whole of the following day. Captain L. has no accurate means of judging of the loss of property sustained, having sailed on the 16th following, but thinks it must be very great, as from two to three hundred stores and dwelling houses, with the greater part of their contents, were consumed The fire, it was thought, had originated in accident.

THE MYSTERIOUS STRANGER. A circumstance occurred during the night of Sir Lionel Smith's dance, which has excited a considerable sensation in Spanish Town, and has since been the source of wonderment, and the general theme of conversation. It appears, that between 9 and 10 o'clock, a field odicer, in the uniform of the Royals, suddenly made his appearance in the ballroom ; but no one observed when, or in what direction he entered. He was about live feet eight inches in heighi, about the age of forty, genteel appearance, in with a florid complexion, and a laughing blue eye ; his regimentals and epaulets appeared as if they bad never been worn. All eyes were upon him, and the general question was who is lie ? þÿ I saw that Sir Lionel observed him, and whispered something to an officer, w ho shook his head The individual, however, appeared unconscious of having attracted the general observation of the company ; but advanced, with the perfect confidence of a well bred man, to a ladv, who arose, placed her arms in his, and joined the dance. The curiosity, in some measure subsided, and the officer danced

several sets ; still, nobody could tell who he was, or where he came from þÿ The Military were quite at a loss to guess, as it was understood that no officer of the Royals was in the island ; and after ihe clock struck 13, the mys-

SOI&iafcJftW'&S AT113 terious stranger suddenly disappeared ; hut in what manner, or by what door he effected his departure, is unknown. Enquires were again set on foot, but without any intelligence having been obtained respecting him. Rumouu with her hundred tongues, was on the alert- Some said that lie drove up from Kingston in a sleigh, drawn by two large blood hounds , hut on enquiring of the owner of the uogs, it appeared that they had not been away from his premises during the night ; and the keeper of the Ferry Toll declared, that no such vehicle passed that evening ; the Toll keeper at the Old Harbour Turnpike was equally positive the stranger had not passed through ; and the wharfinger at Fort Henderson had not seen him land. Others said that it was either Signor Abbondio, Jem Crow, or the Devil. The former, 1 learn, can prove an alibi, but whether Jim Crow or the Devil can, is yet to he learnt. The ladies with whom he danced are positive that he was no immaterial being; they rested on his arm, and distinctly felt the pressure of his hand, though tliev all declare they did not see his feet, as lie wore boots with spurs ; and that, if their partner was Old Nick, he was a very gentlemanly personage. Still the Old Roy may have stuffed his cloven feet into the boots, and wedged them up with straw, to keep them on. However the matter remains, and I suppose ever will, a mystery. C.

Deatii preferred to Dishonor. þÿ During the Irish " reiirn of terror," in 1798, a circumstance occurred, which in the days of Sparta wouid have immortalized the heroine ; it is almost unknown, no pen has ever traced the story. We pause not to inquire into the principles that influenced her ; suffice it that, in common with most of her stamp, she beheld the struggle as one in which liberty warred with tyiannv Her only son had been taken in the act of rebellion, and was condemned, bv marshal law, to death ; she followed the officer, on whose word his life depended, to the place of execution, and besought him to spare the widow's stay ; she knelt in the agony of iter soul, and clasped his knees, while her eye, with the glare of a maniac, fell on her child beside him. The judge was inexorable, the transgressor- must die. Rut, taking advantage of the occasion, he offered life to the culprit on condition of his discovering the members of the association with whom he was connected. The son wavered þÿ the mother rose from her position of humiliation and exclaimed, My " child, my child, if you do, the heaviest curse of your mother shall fall upon you, and the milk of her bosom shall be poison in your veins." He was executed þÿ the pride of her soul enabled her to behold it without a tear þÿ she returned to her home þÿ the support ol her dec lining years had fnllen þÿ the tie that bound her to life had given way þÿ and the evening of the day that saw her lonely and forsaken, left her at rest forever Her heart

had broke in the struggle. þÿ New monthly Belle Asseinhlee. Temper. þÿ Good temper is like a sunny day ; it sheds a brightness over every thing. It is the sweetener of toils, and the soother of disquietude. Every day brings its burthen. The husband goes forth in the morning to his professional studies ; he cannot foresee what trial he may encounter, what failure of hopes, of friendships, or of prospects may meet him, before he returns to his home ; but if he can anticipate there the beaming and hopef ul smile,

an i the soothing attention, he feels that his cross, whatever it might be, will be lightened, and that his domestic happiness is still solute. It is the interest, therefore, as well as the duty of a woman, to cultivate good temper, and to have ever ready some word or look ol cheerfulness of encouragement, or at least ot sv inpathy. A really feeling heart will dictate tl»e conduct which will be most acceptable, will teach the delicacy which times a kindness, as well as renders it, and lot heat sail officious attentions, whilst it ever evinces a readiness to oblige, it need scarcely he said that this temper is of more vaiue than many more brilliant endowments, that it is amongst the lirst recommendations to a woman in every domestic relation, and that especially in that tie which, though the nearest oil earth, is not one of kindred, it is assuredly the most effectual cement of affection. It is not, indeed so much a means of attracting or exciting love, as it is of securing it. In fact, it is scarcely known, until familiarity draws aside the veil of social restraint, and the character, with its real faults and virtues, is unfolded in the privacy of home. þÿ Female Improvement (by Mrs. Sandtord).

We publish this day an extract from the St. Christophers Gazette, relative to the abduction of free people and apprentices to Demerara and Berbice, it will be seen by this extract that gross deception is used towards the unfortunate individuals thus decoyed þÿaway. The Schooner Mary Sharp, came to this Island on a similar errand, having an agent on board, who succeeded in inducing a number of young Mechanics to emigrate to Berbice, under the most flatter ing promises . This vessel arrived here the 1 Ith and sailed again on the 1 4th of February. We understand that several of the individuals who have embarked on this hazardous speculation were warned by the A uthorifies against the risk they incurred in thus allowing themselves to be decoyed away by a stranger ; and we consider it a duty due to the public, as a further warning, to insert the following:

From the St. Christopher Gazette, Feb. 17. Emigration, or rather the speculation in human Jlesh, to which we have before adverted continues ; and on Monday se'nnight, the Sloop Fanny, the property of Mr. Thornton, ailed hence for Demerara. Previous to her leaving this port, a circumstance occurred which has resulted in Mr. Thornton's being bound over to appear at the Sessions to answer an indictment which is to be prelerred against him. We have obtained the particulars that led to this result, and which are as follows : þÿ A woman appeared before K. B. Cleghorm Esq., one of the Special Justices of this Island, on Monday the 6th instant, and stated that the President administering the Government, to whom she bad applied, had sent her to him to say that His Honor wished to see him on the subject of her complaint. Mr. Cleghorn having repaired to Government House, found that the woman had stated that Mr. Thornton was about to send her only children (twok to Demerara, he having purchased the remaining time of their apprenticeship from the parties entitled thereto. A similar complaint having been made on the Raturday previously, by another woman. His Honor directed Mr. ('leghorn to go on board Mr. Thornton's vessel and examine the various contracts which the complaining parties alleged Mr. Thornton to have induced them to enter into. Mr. Jleghorn (accompanied by Mr. Pedder, Private Secretary to the President) accordingly went off with two special constables, and on reaching the tanny was refused admittance on board þÿ in fact, we are

told, wag obstructed in the discharge of this duty by Mr. Thornton and the captain of the vessel, and the insufficiency of the force and the disadvantageous position occupied by Mr. Cleghorn, þÿ being in a boat, and the adverse party in a vessel, with a crew at þÿcommand, at once determined him on not attempting a forcibly entry on board. A petition on parchment from almost all the distinguished literary men in Great Britain, praying the attention of the American Congress to the copy-right law of the United States, and to the establishment of an international copy-right law, Was presented to day by Mr ('lay. A petition from many American authors is in the hands of Mr. Webster, and would have been presented to-day, but for Ins engagements in the Supreme Court. This English petition is probably one of the most valuable collection of English autographs in this country, and would' be quite a temptation for a little thelt if thrown in the way of the autograph hunters of the day. This subject of an international copy-right faw is now attracting much attention here. The justice of it no man here doubts, but it is said that it will make English publications dearer. This I do not credit, for the boot sellers will then share profits with the þÿauthor, and instead of having but one eatch-penny edition, as we arc now likely to have, of English books, we shal' then have two editions, a good readable one with maps, drawings and engravings, as in the English publications, and then another to eatch pennies with. þÿ New hork Express.

Fashionable Society at Vienna. The ladies of Vienna, as 1 said before, are the handsomest in Germany ; for in a re-union of Austrians, Italians, Hungarians, Polish, Bohemians, &c., there is necessarily great variety ; yet the display beauty of i« but scanty compared with that in our own circles. þÿ They are, however, extremely amiable highly accomplished in music, waltzing, and culinary arts; in the latter attainment the German women are preminent, for it forms an essential part of their education ; even, the Empress of Austria makes her husband's coflee, and orders his dinner 'I here is, however, one charm peculiar to the society of Vienna, even in the highest circles the toial absence of ceremony. The soirees usually commence about nine, and are extremely brilliant, when given by any member of the imperial family, as etiquette there obliges the guests to appear in fuil dress, we see stars arid crosses glittering in every direction. 1 do not believe that any people Europe, in are more partial to titles and orders than the Germans, and more especially the Austrians, to which they add an exct ssive fondness for brilliants, displaying them both on the fingers and crhvats, and really I believe that every man in Vienna, from the Prince to the shoe-black wears a ring; the noble has his arms engraved on it, the merchant his initials, the mechanic the device of his trade; know I not if the latter fie universal, but I do know that my shoe maker had a neat little shoe engraved on the massive gold ring that he usually wore. At those re-unions

an Englishman is immediately recognized by the simplicity of his costume, and if we regard thi s as a test of civilization, we should he inclined to assign tiiem high a rank in the scale ; for. assuredly, the lower a nation is sunk in barbarism the more they delight in finery. þÿ Not, however, that 1 mean to insinuate aught against the civilization oi the Germans ; but as the English now give tone to European society, this passion among the Vienna fashionables for decorating their persons is fast losing ground; indeed 1 could not avoid observing, that the most intellectual looking men 1 met with in Vienna society exhibited a splendid display of ribbands and jewels þÿ this was pa'' ticular noticeable in a certain general Count , notorious for his cowardice during the late war, and who now is to be seen at all the public places glittering with military orders. Tne Austrian ladies, strange to say, do not ni oiliest the same fondness lor bejoutene as th ir lords; indeed I thought they exhibited boili negligence and bad taste in the business of liie toilette ; for instance, in arranging the ban , whether the fashion of building a pyramid on the top of the head does not corres" pond with the contour of a German countenance, 1 cannot say, but certainly it struck mc as very unbecoming. How much more simple and graceful is the fashion of wearing the hair floating over the neck and shoulders. Again, stranger, a while contemplating the Vienna belles, would be inclined to conclude

that stays were scarce ; another of his inferences would be, tliat the cavaliers of the ball room where most unpolite to the fair dames, and, although this is merely custom, yet it appears singular to see a belle, after being whirled through the waltz till throughly fatigued, left, however high her rank, to elbow her way through the crowd to a seat, as best she can while Iter ungallant knight pursues the dance with another partner, or mingles with his male þÿacquaintances. SHOCKING EVENT. In a part of the United States the dead are never left alone till the earth is thrown upon them, and. as a friend of the family. 1 had been called upon for this melancholy service on the night proceeding the interment. It was a death which had left a family of broken hearts ; for beneath the sheet which sunk so appaling to the outline of a human form, by a wreck of beauty and of sweetness and beauty, wiiose , loss seemed to the survivers to have darkened the face of tfie earth. The ethereal and touch, ing loveliness of that dying girl, whom 1 had known only as a hopeless victim of consumption, springs up in memory even yet, and mingles with every conception of female beauty. Two ladies, friends of the deceased, were to share my vigils 1 knew them but slightly, and, having read them to sleep an hour after midnight 1 performed my half hourly duty o1 entering the room where the corpse lay, to look after the lights, and then strolled into the garden to enjoy the quiet of the summer night. The flowers were glittering in their pearl drops and the air was breathless. The sight ol the long sheeted corpse, the sudden flare of light as the loiii; snuffs were removed from the candles, the stillness of the close shuttered room, and my own predispositions to invest death with a supernatural interest, had raised my heart to my throat. I walked backwards and forwards in the garden path ; and the black shadows beneath lite lilacs, and even the glitu ring of the glow-worms within them, seemed weird and fearful. The clock stiuck

and 1 re-entered My companions still slept, and 1 passed on to the inner chamber 1 trimmed the lights and stood and looked at the white heap lying so fearlessly still within the shadow of the curtains ; and my blood seemed to freeze. At the moment when 1 was turn, ing away with a strong effort at a more composed lee I ing, a noise like a flutter of wings' ldllowed by a rush and a sudden silence, struck ou my startled ear. The street was as quiet as dralh, and the noise, which was far too audible to be a deception of lite fancy, had come from the side towards an uninhabited wing of the house. My heart stood still. Another in stunt, and the fire screen was dashed down, and a white cat rushed past mc, and with the speed of lightening sprung like a hyaena upon the corpse The flight of a vampyre into the chamber would not have more curdled my veins. A convulsive shudder run cold over me; but recovering myself command. I rushed to the animal (ol' whose horrible appetite for the flesh of the dead I had read incredulously) and attempted to tear her from the body. With her claws fixed in the breast, and a bawl like the wail of an infernal spirit, she crouched fearless upon it, and the stains already upon the sheet convinced me that it would be impossible to remove Iter without shockingly disfiguring the corpse 1 seized it by the throat ; in the hope of choking her ; but, with the first pressure with my fingers, she flew into my face, and the infuriate animal persuaded me> that it w as a contest for lite. Half blinded by

the fury ol her attack, I loosed her for a moment, and she immediately leaped again at the corpse, and had covered her feetand lace with blood before I could recover nty hold upon her. The body was no longer in a situation to he spared, and 1 seized her with a desperate grasp to draw Iter off: but to my horror, the half cox cred and bloody corpse rose upright in her fangs, and, while 1 paused in fear, sat with drooping arms, and head fallen with helpless-

ness over the shoulder, \ears have not removed that fearful spectacle from eyes. The corpse sunk back, and I succeeded throttling in the monster, and threw her at last lifeless ftom the window. I then composed the disturbed limbs ; laid the hair away once more smoothly on th. forehead, and, crossing the hands over the bosom, covered the violated remains, and left them again to their repose. My companions, strangely enough, slept on, and 1 paced the garden walk alone, till the day dawned over the mountains þÿ H Win's Inkling s of Adventure. J

the first year of marriao. This was the first scene approaching to a quarrel which this newly-married couple had had ; it could scarcely be called a quarrel, but verged towards that questionable ground on which quarrels usually commence. There is something very terrible in this first matrimonial jar; itis a point of incalculable consequence to future peace in the conduct oi married life ; and let all women remember that it is their interest to keep their temper in this first instance, whatever they may do afterwards. It is also well to recollect that even in the most fortunate marriages, the first year is not the happiest. þÿ There is much to be learnt cf submission, of bending the will, in minor occasions and trivial circumstances, on the part of the wife, which never happen during couitship. And then, there is the surprise of finding they are the serving, and not the served, irt daily occurrences, to which it requires infinite wisdom and self control to submit. Yet this is much easier to some natures than to others ; and although it may appear paradoxical it is infinitely less difficult to those who do not passionately love than those who do. The latter have not such an altitude to fall from, w hen they enter upon fhe realities of life, with all the trials of temper and all the infirmities of another human being to bear with, as those who supposed perfection in the idol of their worship, and who suddenly have the veil removed, and discover that the tissue of human nature is uneven. All this takes place the

first year of marriage; let that year be well and wisely passed, particularly on the woman's part ; and the rest will probably follow ; but the first year of marriago is not the happiest. þÿ The Devoted.
